item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Emotional feelings usually arise in the heart area, because the emotions are very much concentrated in that area. It's quite extraordinary what you…
item.description:
Mindfulness as a Non-Interfering Internal Monitor

"Emotional feelings usually arise in the heart area, because the emotions are very much concentrated in that area. It's quite extraordinary what you can find there too. Physiologically there is not much in that area. Perhaps there is a nervous plexus there that highlights emotional feelings, although the physical side of it may not be so important at all. Be detached. Keep free of it. Look at it and be mindful. If you’re mindful, it's as though you are standing back and watching it, without interfering. If you do that, nothing much happens. Mindfulness is a kind of a monitor that checks what’s going on without interfering with it. With mindfulness you sometimes feel as though you are standing back and watching the mind, as though from a back seat inside somewhere. Observing from that back seat, you can see clearly what’s happening in the mind, but you don’t interfere in any way."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The primary weapon is mindfulness. When you have mindfulness, you’ll see the kilesas clearly. By seeing them clearly, you’ll know how to apply…
item.description:
Weapons Against the Kilesas and the Definition of Dhamma

"The primary weapon is mindfulness. When you have mindfulness, you’ll see the kilesas clearly. By seeing them clearly, you’ll know how to apply the antidote. Those kilesas rooted in hate can be eliminated by using mettā, or by developing calm through ānāpānasati. Those rooted in greed are countered by using asubha meditation. The asubha method is very effective against greed. For kilesas rooted in delusion, you must rely on your teacher for guidance. Do you need to study the kilesas to actually know what Dhamma is? Yes, you do. The true meaning of Dhamma is very difficult to understand. The word “Dhamma” comes from the Vedic root, dharati, which means the upholder. So Dhamma is the upholder of everything. Dhamma is the great supporter. It’s the truth. It’s the way things work. When you practice Dhamma correctly, you develop in the right direction. If you go against it, you experience constant trouble within yourself. But you cannot really pin Dhamma down and accurately define it. You cannot reach it in that way.",

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "You begin to see things as they truly are. This seeing reveals that nothing can be permanently labeled as true or false; these…
item.description:
The Overlay of the Separate Self

"You begin to see things as they truly are. This seeing reveals that nothing can be permanently labeled as true or false; these are merely concepts we overlay upon experience. What you discover instead is the ceaseless flow of phenomena arising, persisting briefly, and passing away. You notice how your mind creates suffering by resisting this flow, desperately trying to hold on to what is pleasant and push away what is unpleasant. Most significantly, you realize there is no separate self standing apart from all this activity. In truth, the very idea of such a self is just another concept, another overlay upon direct experience. This clarity of knowing is not hidden away in ancient temples... it manifests naturally for anyone who applies these tools with sincere effort and patience.",

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: There is a very distinct difference between opinionatedness and knowledge originating from wisdom. Opinionatedness tends to jump to conclusions without having any facts,…
item.description:
Distinguishing Between Opinionatedness and Knowledge Born of Wisdom

There is a very distinct difference between opinionatedness and knowledge originating from wisdom. Opinionatedness tends to jump to conclusions without having any facts, or without knowing any background. Whereas wisdom searches the whole field, looks the whole way round and searches the background to see the workings of cause and effect. Because of that thoroughness, there is knowing, not mere views and conceited opinions born of the kilesas. It is very important to try to know the kilesas. Kilesas are the enemy, and you should know the enemy. By knowing the enemy, you become aware of when he is likely to attack, so you can understand what defenses are needed. First you must realize that the kilesas are always there. It’s not as though they are sometimes there and sometimes not – they are always there, so there is no time when they’re not. In fact, the citta is completely ruled by the kilesas and under their sway the whole time.

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The precepts are really the definition of the human state. The five precepts are the required minimal behavior for remaining at the level…
item.description:
The Precepts as the Standard for Human Existence

"The precepts are really the definition of the human state. The five precepts are the required minimal behavior for remaining at the level of a human being. If one goes against them or breaks them, to that extent one is going below the human level. Someone who breaks them continually all the time is going down and down and down. This is very bad, because it’s easy to go down but very difficult to get back up. So people should be careful to keep to the precepts as vigorously as possible. People tend to think that taking a drink doesn't matter. It’s true. The actual taking of a drink is not thought to be very important or considered so by the Buddha. He said that the problem is what you do when you're under the influence of alcohol. When you take a drink you’re no longer in full control yourself. Because of that, you can do things that you shouldn’t do at all."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Companionship is very important; the Buddha always stressed that. The things that you meet in your environment—particularly people—are important. If you associate with…
item.description:
The Importance of Spiritual Companionship and Internalizing Criticism

"Companionship is very important; the Buddha always stressed that. The things that you meet in your environment—particularly people—are important. If you associate with people who are always talking Dhamma, then the mind inclines towards Dhamma. If the talk is about the world, then the mind inclines to the world. And your choice of companions is usually influenced by the practice. If the companionship is not right, it is usually because your thoughts are going out all the time. When you think about other people, there is a tendency to be critical of their behavior, which makes developing companionship very difficult. When you turn inward and put the criticism on yourself, that eliminates the problem. And, of course, you should cultivate a friendly compassion towards all beings."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The other way of doing body contemplation is to begin by questioning the nature of the body. “Where does skin come from? What…
item.description:
Investigating the Nature of Body and Pain

"The other way of doing body contemplation is to begin by questioning the nature of the body. “Where does skin come from? What are its characteristics? What happens if I don't wash it? How is it useful? What happens if it peels off? What’s it like? Supposing you cut a piece off? Consider all aspects of the parts that make up the body. This is the way of developing paññā. ...When pain arises during meditation, you must resolve to investigate that pain, and try to figure it out. To be successful in this practice, you must investigate the pain. It’s no use gritting your teeth and bearing it. That won't work. That won't accomplish anything. There is no value in merely enduring pain. You have to start investigating."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: When we speak of moral precepts, we're dealing with something quite practical. They're like the sturdy fences that keep farm animals from wandering…
item.description:
Moral Precepts as Practical Tools Against Unwholesome Kamma

When we speak of moral precepts, we're dealing with something quite practical. They're like the sturdy fences that keep farm animals from wandering onto the road. But here, what we're protecting isn't just physical safety; we're protecting ourselves and others from the harmful actions that spring from an untrained mind. Every action we take, whether it's good or bad, starts in the mind. This is what the Buddha meant by kamma. The results of these actions, what we call vipaka, follow us just as surely as a cart follows the ox that pulls it. I've observed this countless times during my years in Thailand. When someone lacks basic moral restraint, they become an irritant in society. The noble ones, those who have seen the truth of Dhamma, can spot such a person immediately, just as we would notice a rotten mango in a basket of fresh ones. Let me give you a concrete example: in any organization, whether it's a government office, a business, or even a monastery, you'll find that just one or two people who lack moral shame and moral dread can corrupt the whole enterprise. It's rather like finding a cobra in your room. You might think it's sleeping quietly in the corner, but the moment you let your guard down, it strikes.

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "About 33-34 years ago, I was living at a monastery in Lopburi province. I was smoking at the time. So one night, sitting…
item.description:
Renunciation through Internal and External Cessation

"About 33-34 years ago, I was living at a monastery in Lopburi province. I was smoking at the time. So one night, sitting in a hut on the top of the hill, I thought to myself: “Why do I smoke?”. After reflecting on it for awhile, I realized that it was probably because of taṇhā, because of my attachment to tobacco. I knew that the Buddha taught that taṇhā brings dukkha, so I immediately decided that I must stop. I did, and I haven't smoked since. I’m not saying that it’s logically as easy to give up smoking as that. But I had thought many times about giving up smoking, as many smokers do. But that time, I stop. In giving up smoking, it is not enough to just stop smoking cigarettes. You must also give up the very idea of smoking. Because of that, anyone giving up smoking should refrain from even thinking about smoking. If thoughts of cigarettes come into the mind, turn away from them quickly!. By that means, you quit smoking both externally and internally. That is the way to do it."

item.title: A. Paññāvaddho: "At the ultimate stage, the attainment of Nibbāna, the Arahant know is that Dhamma fully inside, and so no longer needs books. Arahants…
item.description:
Signs of Progress and the Role of Enthusiasm (Pīti)

"At the ultimate stage, the attainment of Nibbāna, the Arahant know is that Dhamma fully inside, and so no longer needs books. Arahants will put their understanding in their own words, but when they read the teachings expressed in the language of the books, they clearly understand their meaning. Pīti is one indication [of progress]. Pīti manifests enthusiasm and zest for doing meditation. Pīti arises when the mind starts to become concentrated, which causes increased interest and attention. There is a definite feeling of relaxing into the practice, and not wanting to be distracted. Pīti is a feeling of satisfaction that comes from being absorbed in what you are doing. The arising of pīti shows that the mind is becoming interested in the meditation object, which is a sign that the meditator is developing toward samādhi."
